claim_that_is_false: ISO/IEC 42006 is not an extension of ISO/IEC 17021-1
the_truth: ISO/IEC 42006 specifies additional requirements TO ISO/IEC 17021-1

hits.text: ISO/IEC 42006:2025 specifies requirements for bodies that audit and certify an AIMS, including audit-time determination for certification cycles. It applies to certification bodies, not to organizations conducting first-party audits. The fact that ISO/IEC 42006 references ISO/IEC 42001 does not extend its scope to internal audit planning. Internal audit duration is determined by the organization using the guidance in ISO 19011:2026, scaled to the AIMS scope and complexity. ISO/IEC 17021-1 governs certification bodies generally but does not supersede ISO/IEC 42006 for AIMS certification audits, making that option a genuine but incorrect distractor.
Decline them — ISO/IEC 17021-1 supersedes ISO/IEC 42006, so its time calculations must be used for any AIMS audit.

ISO/IEC 42006 sets requirements for certification bodies auditing and certifying AI management systems, covering competence, impartiality, and audit conduct. ISO/IEC 42001 contains no conformity assessment provisions; it defines what an organization's AIMS must do, not how a certification body must operate. ISO/IEC 17021-1 provides general management system certification body requirements but is not the AI-specific document. ISO/IEC 42006 is a distinct standard, not a sector extension of ISO/IEC 17021-1.

::hook
Two organizations run four AIMS audits a year each. One has an audit programme. The other has a calendar.
::

::concept title="A programme is a set of audits with a purpose, not a set of dates"
ISO 19011:2026 clause 3.5 defines an **audit programme** as arrangements for a set of one or more audits planned for a set period and aimed at a particular purpose.

Three elements, and the last is the one organizations skip. A set of audits is easy. A time frame is easy. **Directed towards a specific purpose** is the part that turns a schedule into a design, and it is what an auditor examining clause 9.2 looks for first.

Clause 5.1 adds that the extent of a programme should follow from how large the auditee is and what kind of body it is, and on the functionality, complexity, type of risks and opportunities, scope, and level of maturity of the management systems to be audited. A programme that would fit any organization of similar size has not been based on the nature of this one.
::

::concept title="Objectives come from the audit client and its context"
ISO 19011:2026 clause 5.2 places responsibility precisely: the **audit client** should ensure that programme objectives are set so they steer how audits are planned and run, and should ensure the programme is implemented effectively.

It then states where they come from. Objectives should line up with the audit client's **strategic direction** and **context**, and support its management system policies and objectives. The clause lists what they can be based on, including:

- the needs and expectations of relevant interested parties, external and internal;
- the characteristics and requirements of processes, products, services and projects, and how those change;
- management system requirements;
- the need to evaluate organizations that are part of the supply chain;
- the auditee's level of performance and level of maturity.

For an AI management system, that list is not abstract. The interested parties include the individuals a system's outputs affect. The characteristics that changed may be a model replaced, a new deployment context, or a jurisdiction the system now operates in. The supply chain is the model provider, the data broker, the inference platform.
::

::concept title="Borrowed objectives cannot direct anything"
Programme objectives written generically - *verify conformity to ISO/IEC 42001*, *maintain certification readiness* - satisfy the letter of having objectives and do none of the work clause 5.2 asks of them.

The test is whether an objective **directs** planning. If two candidate audit plans would both serve the objective equally, the objective is not directing; it is describing. An objective such as *establish whether the impact assessment process is producing results that are actually considered in risk decisions, across the three systems deployed since the last cycle* directs planning: it names what the audit is for, and a plan that does not reach those three systems fails it visibly.

This is also where an auditor gets leverage. Clause 9.2.1 makes the organization's own requirements audit criteria. **A programme objective the organization set for itself is a requirement it set for itself**, and an audit programme that did not pursue its own stated objectives can be found against them.
::

::callout type="pitfall"
An audit programme that repeats last year's schedule with the dates changed has not considered the results of previous audits or the importance of the processes concerned - and ISO/IEC 42001 clause 9.2.2 requires the organization to consider both when establishing the programme. The evidence is the comparison: two consecutive programmes that differ only in dates, over a period in which the AI estate changed.
::

::concept title="Programme objectives and audit objectives are different"
ISO 19011:2026 separates them, and clause 5.5.2 requires that they be consistent with one another.

| | Programme objective (5.2) | Individual audit objective (5.5.2) |
|---|---|---|
| Set by | the audit client | the individual managing the programme |
| Spans | the whole time frame | one audit |
| Answers | what this set of audits is for | what this audit is to accomplish |
| Example | Establish whether AI impact assessment outputs influence risk decisions across the estate | Determine the extent of conformity of the three customer-facing systems to clauses 6.1.4 and 8.4 |

Conflating them produces one of two failures. Either the programme carries only audit-level objectives, so nothing coordinates the set - each audit is defensible and the year adds up to nothing. Or the individual audits carry only the programme objective, so no audit has a scope precise enough for a finding to be tested against.
::

::deep-dive title="Who the audit client is when everyone works for the same organization"
Clause 5.2 assigns the responsibility for programme objectives to the audit client. In an internal audit that role sits inside the organization, and lesson 1 of module 1 established that the audit client can also be the auditee or the individual managing the programme.

That overlap makes a practical question worth asking early: **who, by name, ensured these objectives were established?**

The answer matters because clause 5.2 asks the audit client not only to establish objectives but to ensure the programme is implemented effectively. Where no one holds that role, the usual symptom is a programme that exists on paper and slips in practice - audits deferred, scopes quietly narrowed, findings from the previous cycle never revisited - with no one whose responsibility it was to notice.

ISO/IEC 42001 clause 5.3 requires top management to assign responsibility and authority for reporting on AIMS performance to top management. An audit programme with no identifiable client is often an early indicator that this assignment was made on paper only.
::

::summary
- An audit programme is arrangements for a set of audits over a time frame directed towards a specific purpose - the purpose is what makes it a design.
- Clause 5.2 places programme objectives with the audit client and ties them to its strategic direction and context.
- Objectives that any audit plan would serve equally are describing rather than directing.
- Programme extent should reflect this auditee's size, nature, complexity, risks and maturity.
- Programme objectives direct a set of audits; individual audit objectives state what one audit accomplishes, and must be consistent with them.
- A programme objective the organization set itself is a requirement it set itself, and can be audited against.
::
